claim: Breast cancer genomes have revealed a novel form of mutation showers (kataegis) in which multiple same-strand substitutions at C:G pairs spaced one to several hundred nucleotides apart are clustered over kilobase-sized regions.
source: Breast cancer genomes have revealed a novel form of mutation showers (kataegis) in which multiple same-strand substitutions at C:G pairs spaced one to several hundred nucleotides apart are clustered over kilobase-sized regions, often associated with sites of DNA rearrangement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012) and represents established findings from whole genome sequencing studies.

claim: Kataegis is often associated with sites of DNA rearrangement.
source: Breast cancer genomes have revealed a novel form of mutation showers (kataegis) in which multiple same-strand substitutions at C:G pairs spaced one to several hundred nucleotides apart are clustered over kilobase-sized regions, often associated with sites of DNA rearrangement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012) describing the association between kataegis and DNA rearrangements.

claim: Kataegis can result from AID/APOBEC-catalysed cytidine deamination in the vicinity of DNA breaks.
source: We show kataegis can result from AID/APOBEC-catalysed cytidine deamination in the vicinity of DNA breaks, likely through action on single-stranded DNA exposed during resection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing that expression of AID/APOBEC deaminases in yeast produces kataegis-like mutation patterns.

claim: Kataegis likely occurs through action on single-stranded DNA exposed during resection.
source: We show kataegis can result from AID/APOBEC-catalysed cytidine deamination in the vicinity of DNA breaks, likely through action on single-stranded DNA exposed during resection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing kataegis association with DNA breaks and the known mechanism of AID/APOBEC action on single-stranded DNA.

claim: Cancer-like kataegis can be recapitulated by expression of AID/APOBEC family deaminases in yeast.
source: Cancer-like kataegis can be recapitulated by expression of AID/APOBEC family deaminases in yeast where it largely depends on uracil excision, which generates an abasic site for strand breakage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genome sequencing of yeast transformants expressing AID/APOBEC deaminases.

claim: Kataegis in yeast largely depends on uracil excision.
source: Cancer-like kataegis can be recapitulated by expression of AID/APOBEC family deaminases in yeast where it largely depends on uracil excision, which generates an abasic site for strand breakage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced kataegis in UNG-deficient yeast strains.

claim: Uracil excision generates an abasic site for strand breakage.
source: Cancer-like kataegis can be recapitulated by expression of AID/APOBEC family deaminases in yeast where it largely depends on uracil excision, which generates an abasic site for strand breakage.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of uracil-DNA glycosylase (UNG) function and the processing of abasic sites.

claim: Localized kataegis can be nucleated by an I-SceI-induced break.
source: Localized kataegis can also be nucleated by an I-SceI-induced break.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased kataegis near an I-SceI cut site in yeast.

claim: APOBEC3B and 3A are the deaminases whose mutational signatures are most similar to those of breast cancer kataegic mutations.
source: Genome-wide patterns of APOBEC3-catalyzed deamination in yeast reveal APOBEC3B and 3A as the deaminases whose mutational signatures are most similar to those of breast cancer kataegic mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of mutation contexts between yeast transformants and breast cancer samples.

claim: APOBEC3B/A are implicated in breast cancer hypermutation.
source: Together with expression and functional assays, the results implicate APOBEC3B/A in breast cancer hypermutation and give insight into the mechanism of kataegis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including mutational signature analysis, expression data, and functional assays.

claim: More than half of 21 sequenced breast cancers contained kataegis.
source: Whole genome sequencing of 21 breast cancers recently revealed the presence in more than half the cancers of a novel form of localised hypermutation (termed kataegis) in which clusters of multiple same-strand mutations at C:G pairs are focused on multikilobase-long genomic regions with adjacent mutations within each cluster separated by one to several hundred base pairs (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the prior whole genome sequencing study.

claim: Kataegic mutations occurred nearly exclusively at C residues preceded by a 5′-T.
source: Although the mechanism underlying kataegis is unknown, the fact that the mutations occurred nearly exclusively at C residues preceded by a 5′-T suggested that AID/APOBEC cytidine-DNA deaminases might possibly be involved in the process since these enzymes are sensitive to the 5′-flanking sequence context (Conticello et al., 2007; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior sequencing studies.

claim: AID/APOBEC cytidine-DNA deaminases are sensitive to the 5′-flanking sequence context.
source: Although the mechanism underlying kataegis is unknown, the fact that the mutations occurred nearly exclusively at C residues preceded by a 5′-T suggested that AID/APOBEC cytidine-DNA deaminases might possibly be involved in the process since these enzymes are sensitive to the 5′-flanking sequence context (Conticello et al., 2007; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies characterizing AID/APOBEC sequence preferences.

claim: Members of the AID/APOBEC family of enzymes deaminate cytosine in the context of a single-stranded polynucleotide substrate.
source: Members of the AID/APOBEC family of enzymes (reviewed in Conticello et al., 2007) deaminate cytosine in the context of a single-stranded polynucleotide substrate, and function in adaptive and innate immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article and represents established knowledge about AID/APOBEC function.

claim: AID/APOBEC family members function in adaptive and innate immunity.
source: Members of the AID/APOBEC family of enzymes (reviewed in Conticello et al., 2007) deaminate cytosine in the context of a single-stranded polynucleotide substrate, and function in adaptive and innate immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article and represents established knowledge.

claim: AID acts on C residues in the DNA of the genomic immunoglobulin loci in activated lymphocytes to trigger antibody gene diversification.
source: AID acts on C residues in the DNA of the genomic immunoglobulin loci in activated lymphocytes to trigger antibody gene diversification whereas APOBEC3 family members, of which there are seven in humans, act on C residues in the DNA of viral replication intermediates (usually in the cytoplasm) as part of a host restriction pathway.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about AID function in adaptive immunity.

claim: There are seven APOBEC3 family members in humans.
source: AID acts on C residues in the DNA of the genomic immunoglobulin loci in activated lymphocytes to trigger antibody gene diversification whereas APOBEC3 family members, of which there are seven in humans, act on C residues in the DNA of viral replication intermediates (usually in the cytoplasm) as part of a host restriction pathway.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the number of APOBEC3 genes in humans.

claim: APOBEC3 family members act on C residues in the DNA of viral replication intermediates as part of a host restriction pathway.
source: AID acts on C residues in the DNA of the genomic immunoglobulin loci in activated lymphocytes to trigger antibody gene diversification whereas APOBEC3 family members, of which there are seven in humans, act on C residues in the DNA of viral replication intermediates (usually in the cytoplasm) as part of a host restriction pathway.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about APOBEC3 function in innate immunity.

claim: APOBEC3 family members usually act in the cytoplasm.
source: AID acts on C residues in the DNA of the genomic immunoglobulin loci in activated lymphocytes to trigger antibody gene diversification whereas APOBEC3 family members, of which there are seven in humans, act on C residues in the DNA of viral replication intermediates (usually in the cytoplasm) as part of a host restriction pathway.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the typical subcellular localization of APOBEC3 activity.

claim: Off-target deamination by AID results in nucleotide substitutions and genomic rearrangements in B lymphocyte tumours.
source: Off-target deamination by AID results in nucleotide substitutions and genomic rearrangements in B lymphocyte tumours, some of which are implicated in oncogenesis (reviewed by Gazumyan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Some AID-induced mutations in B lymphocyte tumours are implicated in oncogenesis.
source: Off-target deamination by AID results in nucleotide substitutions and genomic rearrangements in B lymphocyte tumours, some of which are implicated in oncogenesis (reviewed by Gazumyan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: AID is the only member of the AID/APOBEC family known to act physiologically on endogenous nuclear DNA.
source: Although AID is the only member of the AID/APOBEC family known to act physiologically on endogenous nuclear DNA, it is possible that other members of the AID/APOBEC family might occasionally get access to the nucleus and cause cancer-associated genomic damage or mutation (Harris et al., 2002; Beale et al., 2004; Vartanian et al., 2008; Stenglein et al., 2010; Landry et al., 2011; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Nowarski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the physiological roles of AID/APOBEC family members.

claim: Other members of the AID/APOBEC family might occasionally get access to the nucleus and cause cancer-associated genomic damage or mutation.
source: Although AID is the only member of the AID/APOBEC family known to act physiologically on endogenous nuclear DNA, it is possible that other members of the AID/APOBEC family might occasionally get access to the nucleus and cause cancer-associated genomic damage or mutation (Harris et al., 2002; Beale et al., 2004; Vartanian et al., 2008; Stenglein et al., 2010; Landry et al., 2011; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Nowarski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative but supported by multiple citations suggesting this possibility.

claim: All members of the AID/APOBEC family expressed in yeast gave a significant increase in the mutation frequency as judged by the yield of colonies resistant to canavanine.
source: Several members of the AID/APOBEC family members were expressed in yeast and all were found to give a significant increase in the mutation frequency as judged by the yield of colonies resistant to canavanine (CanR) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most CanR colonies had typically accumulated less than 10 point mutations during the period of AID/APOBEC induction and clonal expansion.
source: Genome sequencing, however, revealed that most CanR colonies had typically accumulated less than 10 point mutations (>98% at C:G pairs) during the period of AID/APOBEC induction and clonal expansion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: More than 98% of mutations in AID/APOBEC-expressing yeast were at C:G pairs.
source: Genome sequencing, however, revealed that most CanR colonies had typically accumulated less than 10 point mutations (>98% at C:G pairs) during the period of AID/APOBEC induction and clonal expansion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A hyperactive mutant of AID (AID*) gave a significantly higher mutation load with a median of 25 mutations per genome.
source: A hyperactive mutant of AID (AID*; Wang et al., 2009) gave a significantly higher mutation load (median of 25 mutations per genome).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data and citation to the source of the AID* mutant.

claim: 1078 mutations were identified in AID*-transformants, of which all except 14 were at C:G pairs.
source: We therefore initially focused on the mutations in AID*-transformants (1078 mutations in total, of which all except 14 were at C:G pairs) to see if there were signs of kataegis.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data from AID*-transformants.

claim: The median overall intermutational distance in AID* yeast transformants is 13 kb.
source: While the median overall intermutational distance (IMD) is 13 kb, it is apparent that rather than the mutations being scattered randomly over the genome, mutation distribution is bimodal (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutation distribution in AID* yeast transformants is bimodal.
source: While the median overall intermutational distance (IMD) is 13 kb, it is apparent that rather than the mutations being scattered randomly over the genome, mutation distribution is bimodal (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Singlet mutations in AID* transformants exhibit a median IMD of 156 kb.
source: Dividing the mutations into two groups using k-means cluster analysis (Hartigan and Wong, 1979) reveals that one group exhibit a median IMD of 156 kb with a distribution of distances that is as expected for a set of individual mutations randomly scattered over the yeast genome as judged by Monte Carlo simulation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by k-means cluster analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: Singlet mutations account for 52% of the total mutations in AID* transformants.
source: We designate these as singlet mutations: they account for 52% of the total mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: Proximal mutations in AID* transformants are separated from each other by a median IMD of only 727 bp.
source: The remaining 48% of the mutations are much more closely spaced than would be expected on a random basis. We designate these as proximal mutations, which are separated from each other by a median IMD of only 727 bp with >99% of them being within 8.5 kb of their closest neighbour.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: More than 99% of proximal mutations in AID* transformants are within 8.5 kb of their closest neighbour.
source: The remaining 48% of the mutations are much more closely spaced than would be expected on a random basis. We designate these as proximal mutations, which are separated from each other by a median IMD of only 727 bp with >99% of them being within 8.5 kb of their closest neighbour.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: 75% of the AID*-induced proximal mutations are parts of clusters.
source: Thus, if we define proximal mutations as a pair of mutations that are located <8.5 kb apart (a distance that excludes 99% of the singlet mutations) and define a cluster as a stretch of DNA containing ≥5 proximal mutations, we find that 75% of the AID*-induced proximal mutations are actually parts of clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data using defined criteria for clusters.

claim: Clusters in AID* transformants typically extend over 6–15 kb.
source: These clusters typically extend over 6–15 kb (with the full range detected being 1.8–30 kb) and contain anything up to 26 mutations (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The full range of cluster lengths detected in AID* transformants was 1.8–30 kb.
source: These clusters typically extend over 6–15 kb (with the full range detected being 1.8–30 kb) and contain anything up to 26 mutations (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Clusters in AID* transformants contain up to 26 mutations.
source: These clusters typically extend over 6–15 kb (with the full range detected being 1.8–30 kb) and contain anything up to 26 mutations (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: More than one-third of the AID* transformants analysed (16/40) contain at least one mutation cluster.
source: The level of mutation clustering observed with AID* is such that more than one-third of the transformants analysed (16/40) contain at least one mutation cluster.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data from 40 AID* transformants.

claim: In affected clones, a quarter to two-thirds of all the mutations are concentrated in a small number of clusters that account for <0.2% of the entire genome.
source: In affected clones, a quarter to two-thirds of all the mutations in the cell are concentrated in a small number of clusters that account for <0.2% of the entire genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: Similar clusters were observed in yeast cells transformed with APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B as well as with the hyperactive APOBEC3G mutant APOBEC3G*.
source: Similar clusters were also observed in yeast cells transformed with APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B as well as with the hyperactive APOBEC3G mutant APOBEC3G* (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: The clustered mutations in the various yeast transformants showed a strong tendency towards strand polarity with over 88% of mutations being strand coordinated.
source: Like the cancer kataegis, the clustered mutations in the various yeast transformants showed a strong tendency towards strand polarity; mutations within a cluster occur predominantly at either a C residue or a G residue with over 88% of mutations being strand coordinated (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: 76% of the mutations in the yeast AID* transformants are C→T transitions.
source: Exploring the mutational spectra, we find that the majority (76%) of the mutations in the yeast AID* transformants are C→T transitions, although transversions do occur and these are preferentially associated with the kataegic stretches (Figure 2A and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Transversions are preferentially associated with kataegic stretches in AID* transformants.
source: Exploring the mutational spectra, we find that the majority (76%) of the mutations in the yeast AID* transformants are C→T transitions, although transversions do occur and these are preferentially associated with the kataegic stretches (Figure 2A and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Transversions account for 54% of the kataegic mutations in the AID* transformants but for only 13% of the unclustered substitutions.
source: Transversions account for 54% of the kataegic mutations in the AID* transformants but for only 13% of the unclustered substitutions (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Table 1.

claim: The same bias towards transversion mutations in the kataegic stretches is observed in the APOBEC3A, 3B and 3G* transformants.
source: The same bias towards transversion mutations in the kataegic stretches is also observed in the APOBEC3A, 3B and 3G* transformants (Figure 2A and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: C→T transitions likely arise through direct replication over uracils generated by cytidine deamination.
source: Whereas C→T transitions will likely arise through direct replication over uracils generated by cytidine deamination, transversions are presumably due to replication over abasic sites created through uracil excision by uracil-DNA glycosylase (UNG).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of how uracil in DNA is processed during replication.

claim: Transversions are presumably due to replication over abasic sites created through uracil excision by uracil-DNA glycosylase (UNG).
source: Whereas C→T transitions will likely arise through direct replication over uracils generated by cytidine deamination, transversions are presumably due to replication over abasic sites created through uracil excision by uracil-DNA glycosylase (UNG).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of UNG function and inference from the data.

claim: The transversions exhibit a strong (4- to 10-fold) bias for C→G rather than C→A substitutions.
source: The transversions exhibit a strong (4- to 10-fold) bias for C→G rather than C→A substitutions (Table 1) suggesting that the replication over the abasic site could be catalysed by REV1 since this translesion polymerase (by virtue of its deoxycytidyl nucleotide transferase activity) inserts C opposite abasic sites (Nelson et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data shown in Table 1.

claim: REV1 is a translesion polymerase that inserts C opposite abasic sites by virtue of its deoxycytidyl nucleotide transferase activity.
source: The transversions exhibit a strong (4- to 10-fold) bias for C→G rather than C→A substitutions (Table 1) suggesting that the replication over the abasic site could be catalysed by REV1 since this translesion polymerase (by virtue of its deoxycytidyl nucleotide transferase activity) inserts C opposite abasic sites (Nelson et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work characterizing REV1 function.

claim: Deficiency in either REV1 or UNG led to a dramatic fall in the proportion of transversion mutations.
source: Indeed, deficiency in either REV1 or UNG led to a dramatic fall in the proportion of transversion mutations (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data from REV1 and UNG deficient strains shown in Table 1.

claim: Deficiency in UNG resulted in a fourfold increase in the average total mutation load in AID* transformants.
source: Deficiency in UNG also resulted in a fourfold increase in the average total mutation load in AID* transformants (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data from UNG deficient strains.

claim: The increased mutation load in UNG-deficient cells presumably reflects diminished repair of the AID/APOBEC-generated uracils.
source: Deficiency in UNG also resulted in a fourfold increase in the average total mutation load in AID* transformants (Supplementary file 1B). This presumably reflects diminished repair of the AID/APOBEC-generated uracils.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the known role of UNG in base excision repair.

claim: There was an overall decrease in average total mutation load in AID* transformants of REV1 deficient yeast.
source: There was an overall decrease in average total mutation load in AID* transformants of REV1 deficient yeast that might reflect the possible non-catalytic roles of REV1 during DNA damage repair (Sale et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data from REV1 deficient strains.

claim: The decreased mutation load in REV1 deficient yeast might reflect the possible non-catalytic roles of REV1 during DNA damage repair.
source: There was an overall decrease in average total mutation load in AID* transformants of REV1 deficient yeast that might reflect the possible non-catalytic roles of REV1 during DNA damage repair (Sale et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to prior work on REV1 function.

claim: The increased mutation load in AID* ung1Δ transformants was accompanied by a dramatic shift away from mutational clustering.
source: We found that the increased mutation load in AID* ung1Δ transformants was accompanied by a dramatic shift away from mutational clustering (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The percentage of proximal mutations falls from 48% in AID* wild type cells to 18% in ung1Δ transformants.
source: Despite the fourfold 'increase' in mutation load, the percentage of mutations that are <8.5 kb from their neighbour (proximal mutations) actually 'falls' from accounting for 48% of the AID* mutations in wild type cells to 18% in ung1Δ transformants.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data from wild type and ung1Δ strains.

claim: 274 of the 1064 mutations observed in AID* wild type transformants are found within clusters compared to 28 of the 2088 mutations in the AID* ung1Δ transformants.
source: Similarly, using the same criterion to distinguish clustered mutations in both datasets (≥5 linked mutations separated from their neighbour by <8.5 kb), 274 of the 1064 mutations observed in AID* wild type transformants are found within clusters compared to 28 of the 2088 mutations in the AID* ung1Δ transformants (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: The median overall IMD increases from 13 kb in AID* wild type transformants to 41 kb in the ung1Δ cells despite the increase in mutation load.
source: Thus, the median overall IMD actually 'increases' from 13 kb in AID* wild type transformants to 41 kb in the ung1Δ cells despite the increase in mutation load.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: There is an absolute fall in the amount of kataegis in UNG-deficient cells as judged by the average number of clustered mutations per yeast transformant (6.9 in the wild type background vs 1.5 in the ung1Δ transformants).
source: There is also an absolute fall in the amount of kataegis as judged by either the average number of clustered mutations per yeast transformant (6.9 in the wild type background vs 1.5 in the ung1Δ transformants) or by the frequency of kataegic events (26 kataegic stretches in 40 AID* transformants in the wild type background vs 4 kataegic stretches in 19 AID* transformants in ung1Δ background) (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: The frequency of kataegic events is 26 kataegic stretches in 40 AID* transformants in the wild type background vs 4 kataegic stretches in 19 AID* transformants in ung1Δ background.
source: There is also an absolute fall in the amount of kataegis as judged by either the average number of clustered mutations per yeast transformant (6.9 in the wild type background vs 1.5 in the ung1Δ transformants) or by the frequency of kataegic events (26 kataegic stretches in 40 AID* transformants in the wild type background vs 4 kataegic stretches in 19 AID* transformants in ung1Δ background) (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: Kataegis is substantially reduced in the UNG-deficient background, but not completely lost.
source: Thus, it is evident that kataegis is substantially reduced in the UNG-deficient background, but not completely lost: a few residual clusters (which exhibit evident strand polarity or bipolarity) are still detected (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cleavage at abasic sites by apyrimidinic endonucleases will lead to occasional double-stranded DNA breaks.
source: Cleavage at abasic sites by apyrimidinic endonucleases will lead to occasional double-stranded DNA breaks: kataegis could result from AID/APOBEC deamination of single-stranded DNA exposed during the resection phase of break repair.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of how abasic sites are processed.

claim: Kataegis could result from AID/APOBEC deamination of single-stranded DNA exposed during the resection phase of break repair.
source: Cleavage at abasic sites by apyrimidinic endonucleases will lead to occasional double-stranded DNA breaks: kataegis could result from AID/APOBEC deamination of single-stranded DNA exposed during the resection phase of break repair.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the data.

claim: Induction of I-SceI expression resulted in an increased frequency of deaminase-dependent selectable mutation at the linked CAN1 locus.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Poltoratsky et al., 2010), induction of I-SceI expression resulted in an increased frequency of deaminase-dependent selectable mutation at the linked CAN1 locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with prior work.

claim: In the presence of APOBEC3G*, induction of a double-strand break increases the probability that mutations in its vicinity are kataegic.
source: More importantly, in the presence of APOBEC3G*, induction of a double-strand break increases the probability that mutations in its vicinity are kataegic (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Most of the breast cancers identifiable by rainfall plots as harbouring major regions of kataegis also contain clusters comprising smaller numbers of same-strand nucleotide substitutions at 5′-T-C dinucleotides.
source: Most of the cancers identifiable by rainfall plots as harbouring major regions of kataegis also contain clusters comprising smaller numbers of same-strand nucleotide substitutions at 5′-T-C dinucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: Tumour PD4107a carries a dense array of highly mutated (and transition-restricted) kataegic clusters coincident with extensive genomic rearrangement in a 14 Mb region of chromosome 6.
source: The main outlier is tumour PD4107a which carries a dense array of highly mutated (and transition-restricted) kataegic clusters coincident with extensive genomic rearrangement in a 14 Mb region of chromosome 6 (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The kataegic clusters in the breast cancers are distributed over a similar range of lengths to those detected in the yeast transformants.
source: Overall, the kataegic clusters in the breast cancers are distributed over a similar range of lengths to those detected in the yeast transformants (Figure 3A) but the yeast clusters do typically contain a twofold to fivefold lower density of mutations (a mean inter-mutational distance of 1220 bp within the AID* yeast kataegic stretches compared to 209 bp in PD4107a, 335 bp in PD4103a and 763 bp in PD4199a).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of yeast and breast cancer data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The yeast clusters typically contain a twofold to fivefold lower density of mutations than breast cancer clusters.
source: Overall, the kataegic clusters in the breast cancers are distributed over a similar range of lengths to those detected in the yeast transformants (Figure 3A) but the yeast clusters do typically contain a twofold to fivefold lower density of mutations (a mean inter-mutational distance of 1220 bp within the AID* yeast kataegic stretches compared to 209 bp in PD4107a, 335 bp in PD4103a and 763 bp in PD4199a).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of mutation density in yeast and breast cancer.

claim: The mean inter-mutational distance within the AID* yeast kataegic stretches is 1220 bp.
source: Overall, the kataegic clusters in the breast cancers are distributed over a similar range of lengths to those detected in the yeast transformants (Figure 3A) but the yeast clusters do typically contain a twofold to fivefold lower density of mutations (a mean inter-mutational distance of 1220 bp within the AID* yeast kataegic stretches compared to 209 bp in PD4107a, 335 bp in PD4103a and 763 bp in PD4199a).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome sequencing data.

claim: The mean inter-mutational distance in breast cancer kataegic stretches is 209 bp in PD4107a, 335 bp in PD4103a and 763 bp in PD4199a.
source: Overall, the kataegic clusters in the breast cancers are distributed over a similar range of lengths to those detected in the yeast transformants (Figure 3A) but the yeast clusters do typically contain a twofold to fivefold lower density of mutations (a mean inter-mutational distance of 1220 bp within the AID* yeast kataegic stretches compared to 209 bp in PD4107a, 335 bp in PD4103a and 763 bp in PD4199a).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data.

claim: In tumours PD4103a, PD4107a and PD4199a, over 91% of the kataegic C mutations are preceded by a T.
source: In tumours PD4103a, PD4107a and PD4199a, over 91% of the kataegic C mutations are preceded by a T (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: The sensitivity to the identity of the base at position −2 in breast cancer kataegic mutations is exceedingly mild.
source: However, any sensitivity to the identity of the base at position −2 is exceedingly mild (average across the kataegic stretches in these three tumours is A:C:G:T = 32:20:19:29 compared to the human genome average of 30:20:20:30) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average base composition at position −2 across the kataegic stretches in tumours PD4103a, PD4107a and PD4199a is A:C:G:T = 32:20:19:29.
source: However, any sensitivity to the identity of the base at position −2 is exceedingly mild (average across the kataegic stretches in these three tumours is A:C:G:T = 32:20:19:29 compared to the human genome average of 30:20:20:30) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data.

claim: The human genome average base composition at position −2 of TC dinucleotides is A:C:G:T = 30:20:20:30.
source: However, any sensitivity to the identity of the base at position −2 is exceedingly mild (average across the kataegic stretches in these three tumours is A:C:G:T = 32:20:19:29 compared to the human genome average of 30:20:20:30) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the human genome sequence.

claim: None of the deaminases analysed to date (AID, APOBEC1, APOBEC3C, 3DE, 3F and 3G) has been shown to exhibit a preference that accords with the breast cancer kataegic mutations.
source: However, none of the deaminases analysed to date (AID, APOBEC1, APOBEC3C, 3DE, 3F and 3G) has been shown to exhibit a preference that accords with the breast cancer kataegic mutations.
evidence: This claim is based on review of prior studies characterizing deaminase sequence preferences.

claim: AID prefers A/G at position −1.
source: Their flanking sequence preferences (reviewed in Conticello et al., 2007) are either radically different (e.g., AID prefers A/G at −1; APOBEC3G prefers C at −1) or else they do not show the high (>90%) preference for T at −1 coupled to a relative indifference to the base at −2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: APOBEC3G prefers C at position −1.
source: Their flanking sequence preferences (reviewed in Conticello et al., 2007) are either radically different (e.g., AID prefers A/G at −1; APOBEC3G prefers C at −1) or else they do not show the high (>90%) preference for T at −1 coupled to a relative indifference to the base at −2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: With AID, APOBEC3C and APOBEC3G the yeast data essentially confirm the previously identified sensitivity to nucleotides located at positions −1 and −2.
source: With AID, APOBEC3C and APOBEC3G the yeast data essentially confirm the previously identified sensitivity to nucleotides located at positions −1 and −2 (AID: 5′-WRC, APOBEC3C: 5′-TYC, APOBEC3G: 5′-CCC) whilst allowing more precise quantitation of the degree of preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast transformants.

claim: AID has a sequence preference of 5′-WRC.
source: With AID, APOBEC3C and APOBEC3G the yeast data essentially confirm the previously identified sensitivity to nucleotides located at positions −1 and −2 (AID: 5′-WRC, APOBEC3C: 5′-TYC, APOBEC3G: 5′-CCC) whilst allowing more precise quantitation of the degree of preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast transformants.

claim: APOBEC3C has a sequence preference of 5′-TYC.
source: With AID, APOBEC3C and APOBEC3G the yeast data essentially confirm the previously identified sensitivity to nucleotides located at positions −1 and −2 (AID: 5′-WRC, APOBEC3C: 5′-TYC, APOBEC3G: 5′-CCC) whilst allowing more precise quantitation of the degree of preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast transformants.

claim: APOBEC3G has a sequence preference of 5′-CCC.
source: With AID, APOBEC3C and APOBEC3G the yeast data essentially confirm the previously identified sensitivity to nucleotides located at positions −1 and −2 (AID: 5′-WRC, APOBEC3C: 5′-TYC, APOBEC3G: 5′-CCC) whilst allowing more precise quantitation of the degree of preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast transformants.

claim: Both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B strongly prefer a T at position −1 (91%).
source: With regard to APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, the results reveal that (consistent with earlier studies on APOBEC3B; Bishop et al., 2004), both enzymes strongly prefer a T at position −1 (91%).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast transformants and is consistent with prior work.

claim: Unlike other deaminases, both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B show mild discrimination with regard to the bases located at position −2.
source: However, the yeast studies reveal that unlike other deaminases, both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B show mild discrimination with regard to the bases located at position −2 (APOBEC3A, A:C:G:T = 25:26:7:42; APOBEC3B, A:C:G:T = 35:14:20:31) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast transformants shown in Figure 3B.

claim: APOBEC3A has a position −2 base preference of A:C:G:T = 25:26:7:42.
source: However, the yeast studies reveal that unlike other deaminases, both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B show mild discrimination with regard to the bases located at position −2 (APOBEC3A, A:C:G:T = 25:26:7:42; APOBEC3B, A:C:G:T = 35:14:20:31) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast transformants shown in Figure 3B.

claim: APOBEC3B has a position −2 base preference of A:C:G:T = 35:14:20:31.
source: However, the yeast studies reveal that unlike other deaminases, both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B show mild discrimination with regard to the bases located at position −2 (APOBEC3A, A:C:G:T = 25:26:7:42; APOBEC3B, A:C:G:T = 35:14:20:31) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast transformants shown in Figure 3B.

claim: APOBEC3B has a signature that fits extremely well with the kataegis in PD4107a and PD4103a (p values in both cases <0.005).
source: Comparing the contexts of the mutations obtained with the individual deaminases in yeast to those of the kataegic mutations in the cancers reveals that APOBEC3B has a signature that fits extremely well with the kataegis in PD4107a and PD4103a whereas APOBEC3A fits better with PD4199a (p values in all three cases <0.005) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of mutation contexts shown in Figure 3D.

claim: APOBEC3A fits better with PD4199a kataegis (p value <0.005).
source: Comparing the contexts of the mutations obtained with the individual deaminases in yeast to those of the kataegic mutations in the cancers reveals that APOBEC3B has a signature that fits extremely well with the kataegis in PD4107a and PD4103a whereas APOBEC3A fits better with PD4199a (p values in all three cases <0.005) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of mutation contexts shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A marked bias towards a 5′-T is seen amongst the individual singlet C mutations in several of the breast tumours (e.g., PD4199a, PD4005a and PD4120a).
source: Interestingly, a marked bias towards a 5′-T is also seen amongst the individual singlet C mutations in several of the breast tumours (e.g., PD4199a, PD4005a and PD4120a; Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: APOBEC3A has been shown to be capable of causing genomic damage in mammalian cells.
source: Although APOBEC3A has been shown to be capable of causing genomic damage in mammalian cells (Vartanian et al., 2008; Stenglein et al., 2010; Landry et al., 2011), the same has not been shown for APOBEC3B.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Induction of APOBEC3B expression in stably transfected human KBM7 cells results in loss of viability.
source: We find that induction of APOBEC3B expression in stably transfected human KBM7 cells (like that of APOBEC3A) results in loss of viability as well as in genomic DNA damage as judged by the induction of γH2AX (a marker of the DNA damage response) and of 53BP1 foci (which identify DNA breaks) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Induction of APOBEC3B expression in stably transfected human KBM7 cells results in genomic DNA damage as judged by the induction of γH2AX.
source: We find that induction of APOBEC3B expression in stably transfected human KBM7 cells (like that of APOBEC3A) results in loss of viability as well as in genomic DNA damage as judged by the induction of γH2AX (a marker of the DNA damage response) and of 53BP1 foci (which identify DNA breaks) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: γH2AX is a marker of the DNA damage response.
source: We find that induction of APOBEC3B expression in stably transfected human KBM7 cells (like that of APOBEC3A) results in loss of viability as well as in genomic DNA damage as judged by the induction of γH2AX (a marker of the DNA damage response) and of 53BP1 foci (which identify DNA breaks) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about γH2AX function.

claim: Induction of APOBEC3B expression in stably transfected human KBM7 cells results in induction of 53BP1 foci.
source: We find that induction of APOBEC3B expression in stably transfected human KBM7 cells (like that of APOBEC3A) results in loss of viability as well as in genomic DNA damage as judged by the induction of γH2AX (a marker of the DNA damage response) and of 53BP1 foci (which identify DNA breaks) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: 53BP1 foci identify DNA breaks.
source: We find that induction of APOBEC3B expression in stably transfected human KBM7 cells (like that of APOBEC3A) results in loss of viability as well as in genomic DNA damage as judged by the induction of γH2AX (a marker of the DNA damage response) and of 53BP1 foci (which identify DNA breaks) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about 53BP1 function.

claim: APOBEC3B shows the highest and broadest pattern of expression among APOBEC3s in breast cancer cell-lines.
source: RNA analysis revealed that although several APOBEC3s can be expressed in individual breast cancer cell-lines, the highest and broadest pattern of expression was evident with APOBEC3B (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The expression of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B in some of the breast cancer cell-lines could be enhanced by treatment with phorbol ester or interferon alpha.
source: Consistent with studies in other cell-types (Madsen et al., 1999; Koning et al., 2009; Stenglein et al., 2010), the expression of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B in some of the breast cancer cell-lines could be enhanced by treatment with phorbol ester or interferon alpha.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: The stimulation of local kataegis in yeast by the induction of an I-SceI break indicates that the process occurs during DNA break repair.
source: The stimulation of local kataegis in yeast by the induction of an I-SceI break indicates that the process occurs during DNA break repair, most likely by AID/APOBEC-catalysed deamination of cytidines exposed on single-stranded DNA during the resection phase of homology-mediated repair.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data showing increased kataegis near I-SceI-induced breaks.

claim: Kataegis most likely occurs by AID/APOBEC-catalysed deamination of cytidines exposed on single-stranded DNA during the resection phase of homology-mediated repair.
source: The stimulation of local kataegis in yeast by the induction of an I-SceI break indicates that the process occurs during DNA break repair, most likely by AID/APOBEC-catalysed deamination of cytidines exposed on single-stranded DNA during the resection phase of homology-mediated repair.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data and knowledge of DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: The lengths of the kataegic stretches (mostly in the range 6–15 kb) are in the same order as the extent of resection observed during yeast DNA break repair.
source: The lengths of the kataegic stretches (mostly in the range 6–15 kb) are in the same order as the extent of resection observed during yeast DNA break repair (reviewed in Paull, 2010) although the occurrence and detection of kataegis is likely to bias towards longer stretches.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of kataegis data with cited review of DNA resection.

claim: The distances separating adjacent mutations within the yeast kataegic stretches (averaging about 1.2 kb in the AID* dataset) might in part reflect that the deaminase both jumps and slides on ssDNA, acting with possibly low efficiency at each encountered cytidine.
source: The distances separating adjacent mutations within the yeast kataegic stretches (averaging about 1.2 kb in the AID* dataset) might in part reflect that the deaminase both jumps and slides on ssDNA, acting with possibly low efficiency at each encountered cytidine as proposed by Goodman (Chelico et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to prior work on deaminase mechanism.

claim: In the absence of an induced double-strand break, kataegis in AID/APOBEC-expressing yeast was greatly dependent on UNG.
source: In the absence of an induced double-strand break, kataegis in AID/APOBEC-expressing yeast was greatly dependent on UNG, likely reflecting that kataegis under these circumstances was dependent on breaks generated through the processing of abasic sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from UNG-deficient strains.

claim: Kataegis in the absence of an induced double-strand break was likely dependent on breaks generated through the processing of abasic sites.
source: In the absence of an induced double-strand break, kataegis in AID/APOBEC-expressing yeast was greatly dependent on UNG, likely reflecting that kataegis under these circumstances was dependent on breaks generated through the processing of abasic sites.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the UNG-dependence of kataegis and knowledge of abasic site processing.

claim: Some residual kataegis is still observed in the absence of UNG, which might well reflect that breaks will occasionally occur spontaneously through other means.
source: That some residual kataegis is still observed in the absence of UNG might well reflect that breaks will occasionally occur spontaneously through other means.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on the observation of residual kataegis in UNG-deficient cells.

claim: The finding that a double-strand break can be the nucleating lesion for kataegis in this yeast experimental system is consistent with the close association of kataegis and rearrangements in breast cancer.
source: The finding that a double-strand break can be the nucleating lesion for kataegis in this yeast experimental system is consistent with the close association of kataegis and rearrangements in breast cancer (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is an inference connecting yeast experimental data with breast cancer observations.

claim: It is probable that APOBEC-catalysed kataegic deamination in exposed stretches of single-stranded DNA in the cancer cells might itself lead to DNA breaks.
source: Whereas the yeast data demonstrate that double-strand breaks can nucleate kataegis, it is probable that APOBEC-catalysed kataegic deamination in exposed stretches of single-stranded DNA in the cancer cells might itself lead to DNA breaks.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the mechanism of deamination and abasic site processing.

claim: Recombinational repair of double-strand breaks in yeast has long been known to be associated with an increased frequency of local mutations with implication of error-prone polymerases.
source: It has long been known that recombinational repair of double-strand breaks in yeast is associated with an increased frequency of local mutations with implication of error-prone polymerases (Strathern et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The signatures of the mutations associated with the I-SceI break implicate APOBEC3 activity rather than error-prone polymerases as the source of mutations during the double-strand break repair.
source: In our experiments, the signatures of the mutations associated with the I-SceI break (see Figure 2D legend) implicate APOBEC3 activity rather than error-prone polymerases as the source of mutations during the double-strand break repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of mutation signatures in I-SceI experiments.

claim: Gordenin and colleagues have shown that extensive clusters of mutations can be induced in yeast by alkylating agents acting on single-stranded DNA.
source: More recently Gordenin and colleagues have shown that extensive clusters of mutations can be induced in yeast by alkylating agents acting on single-stranded DNA (Roberts et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The AID/APOBEC-mediated kataegic hypermutation can be viewed as a specialised, albeit dramatic, example of localised hypermutation caused by exposure of single-stranded DNA during homologous recombination.
source: Thus, the AID/APOBEC-mediated kataegic hypermutation, driven by these endogenous mutagens, can be viewed as a specialised, albeit dramatic, example of localised hypermutation caused by exposure of single-stranded DNA during homologous recombination, along the lines proposed by Roberts (Roberts et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on the experimental data and comparison with prior work.

claim: Transversions in yeast are specifically associated with kataegic stretches whereas the unclustered mutations in the same cells are restricted to transitions.
source: It is striking that transversions in yeast are specifically associated with kataegic stretches whereas the unclustered mutations in the same cells are restricted to transitions.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of mutation spectra in yeast transformants.

claim: The singlet uracils largely encounter UNG as part of the base-excision repair process (which would be non-mutagenic); the C→T transition mutations would be the result of direct replication over the non-excised uracil.
source: The reason for this is a matter for speculation but we suspect the singlet uracils largely encounter UNG as part of the base-excision repair process (which would be non-mutagenic); the C→T transition mutations would be the result of direct replication over the non-excised uracil.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on knowledge of base excision repair mechanisms.

claim: The action of UNG on uracil in a stretch of exposed single-stranded DNA may yield an abasic site that is replicated over by a translesion polymerase rather than repaired.
source: In contrast, the action of UNG on uracil in a stretch of exposed single-stranded DNA may yield an abasic site that is replicated over by a translesion polymerase rather than repaired.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference about DNA repair in different contexts.

claim: Other processes that cause significant exposure of single-stranded DNA (e.g., DNA spooling caused by replication fork stalling; R-loop structures generated during transcription of suitable target sequences) could predispose to kataegis.
source: One can well imagine that other processes that cause significant exposure of single-stranded DNA (e.g., DNA spooling caused by replication fork stalling [Lopes et al., 2006]; R-loop structures generated during transcription of suitable target sequences [Aguilera and Gómez-González, 2008]) could predispose to kataegis.
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to prior work on processes that expose single-stranded DNA.

claim: The kataegic stretches in breast cancers display a twofold to fivefold higher average mutation density than yeast, which could reflect differences in deaminase activity in the two organisms.
source: Comparison of the yeast and breast cancer data reveals that the kataegic stretches in both sets extend over a similar range of lengths but with the cancer kataegis displaying a twofold to fivefold higher average mutation density. This could reflect differences in deaminase activity in the two organisms.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on comparison of mutation densities.

claim: Those cancers which harbour kataegic stretches comprising larger numbers of mutations additionally contain multiple clusters with smaller numbers of T-C mutations.
source: It also appears that those cancers which harbour kataegic stretches comprising larger numbers of mutations additionally contain multiple clusters with smaller numbers of T-C mutations (Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: The marked bias towards a 5′-T seen amongst some cancer singlet C mutations suggests that kataegis might be signalling a much wider implication of APOBEC-mediated deamination in genome-wide mutagenesis in some tumours.
source: The marked bias towards a 5′-T seen amongst some cancer singlet C mutations suggests that kataegis might be signalling a much wider implication of APOBEC-mediated deamination in genome-wide mutagenesis in some tumours.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from mutation signature analysis.

claim: The mutation data obtained in yeast reveal APOBEC3B and APOBEC3A as the only deaminases characterised whose target specificity matches the breast cancer kataegic mutations.
source: The mutation data obtained in yeast reveal APOBEC3B and APOBEC3A as the only deaminases characterised whose target specificity matches the breast cancer kataegic mutations, arguing very strongly for an involvement of these deaminases in cancer kataegis.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of mutation contexts between yeast and breast cancer.

claim: The implication of APOBEC3A fits with data from others revealing that enforced expression of APOBEC3A (as well as APOBEC3C and 3H) can lead to mutation of human papilloma viral DNA.
source: The implication of APOBEC3A fits with data from others revealing that enforced expression of APOBEC3A (as well as APOBEC3C and 3H) can lead to mutation of human papilloma viral DNA (Vartanian et al., 2008) as well as of transfected plasmid DNA (Stenglein et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A has been shown to lead to genomic damage in the nucleus.
source: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A has also been shown to lead to genomic damage in the nucleus (Landry et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: After submission of this manuscript, Burns et al., have demonstrated that APOBEC3B expression also correlates with a T-C mutator phenotype in many primary breast cancer tumours.
source: Furthermore, after submission of this manuscript, Burns et al., have demonstrated that APOBEC3B expression also correlates with a T-C mutator phenotype in many primary breast cancer tumours (Burns et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to work published after manuscript submission.

claim: APOBEC3B and/or APOBEC3A are the deaminases likely responsible for the breast cancer hypermutation.
source: Thus, APOBEC3B and/or APOBEC3A are the deaminases likely responsible for the breast cancer hypermutation although it remains possible that other APOBEC3s might contribute to genome mutation in other tumours.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence including mutation signatures, expression data, and functional assays.

claim: It remains possible that other APOBEC3s might contribute to genome mutation in other tumours.
source: Thus, APOBEC3B and/or APOBEC3A are the deaminases likely responsible for the breast cancer hypermutation although it remains possible that other APOBEC3s might contribute to genome mutation in other tumours.
evidence: This claim is speculative and acknowledges the possibility of other APOBEC3s being involved in other cancer types.

claim: Double strand breaks are a common feature of tumour development.
source: With regard specifically to kataegis, given that double strand breaks are a common feature of tumour development, it will obviously be interesting to discover whether whole genome sequencing of other tumour types also reveals evidence of kataegic hypermutation and whether, in light of the fact that the AID/APOBEC family has undergone considerable expansion in primates, such kataegic hypermutation might also have contributed more generally to recent genome evolution.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: The AID/APOBEC family has undergone considerable expansion in primates.
source: With regard specifically to kataegis, given that double strand breaks are a common feature of tumour development, it will obviously be interesting to discover whether whole genome sequencing of other tumour types also reveals evidence of kataegic hypermutation and whether, in light of the fact that the AID/APOBEC family has undergone considerable expansion in primates, such kataegic hypermutation might also have contributed more generally to recent genome evolution.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the evolution of the AID/APOBEC gene family.
